questions.subject: endo
questions.title: Ambient temperature at which sweating begins
questions.question: Regarding sweat secretion, which one of the following statements is correct?

options.A: It is a passive process that does not require energy
options.B: Sweat glands are stimulated by sympathetic noradrenergic fibres
options.C: It starts when the environmental temperature reaches about 32-34 degrees C
options.D: Increased humidity of the air increases the evaporation of sweat

explanations.A: Incorrect. Sweat secretion is an active secretory process: the secretory coil actively pumps out an isotonic primary secretion, and the duct then actively reabsorbs sodium and chloride, both requiring metabolic energy.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Eccrine sweat glands are an exception among sympathetic targets: they are innervated by sympathetic fibres that release acetylcholine (cholinergic), not noradrenaline.
explanations.C: Correct. Thermoregulatory sweating becomes an effective heat-loss mechanism once the environmental temperature rises to roughly 32-34 degrees C, the point at which radiation and convection can no longer dissipate the body's heat load. Below this range heat is lost mainly by radiation and convection, so sweating contributes little. Above it, evaporation of sweat becomes the body's principal avenue for losing heat.
explanations.D: Incorrect. High ambient humidity reduces, rather than increases, the evaporation of sweat, because the water-vapour gradient between skin and air is small; this is why humid heat feels more oppressive and impairs cooling.

questions.learning_objective: State that thermoregulatory sweating begins at an ambient temperature of about 32-34 degrees C and is a cholinergically driven active process.

questions.title: Mediator of tubuloglomerular feedback from the macula densa
questions.question: In the process of tubuloglomerular feedback, which molecule is released by macula densa cells to constrict the afferent arteriole when the tubular flow (renal blood flow) is increased?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Renin is released from the juxtaglomerular granular cells in response to low perfusion; it is not the paracrine signal the macula densa uses to constrict the afferent arteriole.
explanations.B: Correct. When a rise in GFR delivers more NaCl to the macula densa, the increased NaCl uptake makes these cells release adenosine (with ATP), which acts on A1 receptors of the adjacent afferent arteriolar smooth muscle to cause vasoconstriction. This lowers the glomerular hydrostatic pressure and returns GFR toward normal, the essence of tubuloglomerular feedback. Adenosine is therefore the local vasoconstrictor mediator in this reflex.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Angiotensin II is a circulating/locally generated vasoconstrictor that preferentially constricts the efferent arteriole; it is not the macula densa's paracrine signal onto the afferent arteriole in tubuloglomerular feedback.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Nitric oxide is a vasodilator that opposes tubuloglomerular feedback by relaxing the afferent arteriole, the opposite of the constrictor action being asked about.

questions.learning_objective: Identify adenosine as the macula densa mediator that constricts the afferent arteriole in tubuloglomerular feedback.

questions.title: Definition of filtration fraction
questions.question: Which of the following is correct about the filtration fraction?

options.A: It is the ratio of the glomerular filtration rate to the renal plasma flow
options.B: It is the volume of plasma filtered by one kidney per minute
options.C: It is the volume of plasma filtered by the two kidneys per minute
options.D: It is the percentage of blood converted to glomerular filtrate by one kidney per minute

explanations.A: Correct. The filtration fraction is defined as GFR divided by renal plasma flow (FF = GFR/RPF), normally about 0.2, meaning roughly one-fifth of the plasma reaching the glomeruli is filtered. It expresses how efficiently plasma is filtered rather than an absolute volume. A change in efferent tone or plasma protein concentration alters the filtration fraction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The volume of plasma filtered per minute is the glomerular filtration rate itself, not the filtration fraction, which is a dimensionless ratio.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This again describes an absolute filtered volume (GFR), not the ratio of filtered plasma to plasma delivered.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The filtration fraction is calculated from plasma, not whole blood, and it is a ratio of GFR to renal plasma flow rather than a percentage of blood filtered.

questions.learning_objective: Define the filtration fraction as GFR divided by renal plasma flow (about 0.2).

questions.title: Determinants of glomerular filtration rate (untrue statement)
questions.question: Under normal conditions all of the following statements regarding the glomerular filtration rate are correct EXCEPT:

options.A: The colloid osmotic pressure of the plasma proteins equals approximately 32 mmHg
options.B: The hydrostatic pressure in Bowman's capsule equals approximately 18 mmHg
options.C: An increase in the afferent arteriolar tone increases the glomerular filtration rate
options.D: The net filtration pressure equals approximately 10 mmHg

explanations.A: Incorrect as the answer (the statement is true). The plasma colloid osmotic (oncotic) pressure opposing filtration is about 32 mmHg, one of the standard Starling forces across the glomerular membrane.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the answer (the statement is true). The hydrostatic pressure within Bowman's capsule is approximately 18 mmHg and opposes filtration.
explanations.C: Correct (this is the untrue statement). Increasing the afferent arteriolar tone (constriction) reduces glomerular blood flow and lowers the glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure, so it decreases, not increases, the GFR. Because the question asks for the incorrect statement, this reversed relationship is the answer. Afferent constriction lowers GFR, whereas efferent constriction tends to raise it.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the answer (the statement is true). The net filtration pressure is about 10 mmHg (roughly 60 glomerular hydrostatic minus 32 oncotic minus 18 capsular), the small positive force that drives filtration.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that increased afferent arteriolar tone lowers, not raises, the GFR, and recall the normal Starling pressures.

questions.title: Nephron segment impermeable to water
questions.question: Which of the following renal sites is characterized by having no permeability to water?

options.B: Thin descending limb of the loop of Henle
options.D: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle

explanations.A: Incorrect. The collecting duct's water permeability is variable but present, becoming high under the influence of ADH through aquaporin-2 insertion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The thin descending limb is highly permeable to water, which passively leaves it into the hyperosmotic medulla, concentrating the tubular fluid.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The late distal tubule and collecting system are water-permeable in an ADH-dependent manner, so they do not qualify as impermeable.
explanations.D: Correct. The thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle is essentially impermeable to water while it actively reabsorbs NaCl through the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter. This 'diluting segment' therefore separates solute from water, generating dilute tubular fluid and depositing solute in the medullary interstitium. Its water impermeability is central to the countercurrent multiplier that concentrates the urine.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the thick ascending limb of Henle as the water-impermeable diluting segment that reabsorbs NaCl.

questions.title: Control of water balance and the action of ADH
questions.question: Regarding the control of water balance by the kidneys, which one of the following statements is correct?

options.A: The renal medulla has an osmotic gradient that decreases from the cortico-medullary border towards the papilla
options.B: ADH is secreted by the anterior pituitary in response to a fall in blood osmolality
options.C: A normal person cannot produce urine with an osmolality greater than 300 mOsmol/kg
options.D: ADH acts on the principal cells of the collecting ducts to increase their permeability to water

explanations.A: Incorrect. The medullary osmotic gradient increases, not decreases, from the cortico-medullary junction (about 300 mOsmol/kg) towards the papilla (up to about 1200 mOsmol/kg).
explanations.B: Incorrect. ADH is synthesised in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior (not anterior) pituitary, and its secretion is stimulated by a rise in plasma osmolality, not a fall.
explanations.C: Incorrect. With maximal ADH action a normal person can concentrate urine well above plasma, to around 1200 mOsmol/kg, far exceeding 300 mOsmol/kg.
explanations.D: Correct. ADH (vasopressin) binds V2 receptors on the basolateral membrane of collecting-duct principal cells, raising cyclic AMP and inserting aquaporin-2 water channels into the apical membrane. This increases the water permeability of the collecting duct, allowing water to be reabsorbed down the medullary osmotic gradient and the urine to be concentrated. Loss of this action (as in diabetes insipidus) produces large volumes of dilute urine.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that ADH raises collecting-duct principal-cell water permeability via aquaporin-2 to concentrate the urine.

questions.title: Mechanism of proximal tubular hydrogen secretion
questions.question: Hydrogen ion secretion in the proximal convoluted tubule occurs mainly by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Co-transport would move H+ and Na+ in the same direction, whereas proximal H+ secretion moves H+ into the lumen while Na+ moves into the cell, i.e. counter-transport, not co-transport.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The proximal H+ secretion is not primary active transport; it does not hydrolyse ATP directly at the exchanger but is driven secondarily by the sodium gradient.
explanations.C: Correct. In the proximal tubule most H+ is secreted by the apical Na+/H+ exchanger (NHE3), a secondary active antiporter (counter-transport). The inwardly directed sodium gradient, maintained by the basolateral Na-K ATPase, provides the energy that drives H+ out into the lumen in exchange for Na+ entering the cell. This couples sodium reabsorption to hydrogen secretion and to bicarbonate reclamation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Secretion against the concentration gradient into the lumen cannot occur by simple passive diffusion; it requires the sodium-coupled exchanger.

questions.learning_objective: Describe proximal H+ secretion as secondary active Na+/H+ counter-transport driven by the sodium gradient.

questions.title: Acidification of urine and urinary buffers
questions.question: Regarding acidification of the urine by the renal tubules, which one of the following statements is correct?

options.A: The late distal tubules and collecting ducts are responsible for about 10% of bicarbonate reabsorption but cannot generate new bicarbonate
options.B: Secreted H+ is buffered by ammonia (NH3) in the distal tubule and collecting duct, forming ammonium
options.C: Secreted H+ reacts with NaH2PO4 in the tubular fluid to give Na2HPO4
options.D: H+ is secreted into the tubular fluid by the principal cells of the distal tubule and collecting duct

explanations.A: Incorrect. The distal nephron does generate new bicarbonate as it secretes H+ against buffers; the statement wrongly denies this new-bicarbonate generation that titratable acid and ammonium excretion accomplish.
explanations.B: Correct. In the distal tubule and collecting duct, secreted H+ combines with ammonia (NH3) that has diffused from the tubular cells to form ammonium (NH4+), which is trapped in the lumen and excreted. This ammonia buffer system, together with phosphate, allows the kidney to excrete a large acid load and generate new bicarbonate. Ammonium excretion is the main adaptive route for eliminating acid in chronic acidosis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The phosphate buffer works the other way round: secreted H+ reacts with Na2HPO4 (dibasic) to form NaH2PO4 (monobasic), the titratable acid, so the reaction as written is reversed.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Distal H+ secretion is performed by the alpha-intercalated cells (via an apical H+ ATPase and H+/K+ ATPase), not by the principal cells, which handle Na+, K+ and water.

questions.learning_objective: State that secreted H+ is buffered by ammonia to form ammonium in the distal nephron, a key route of acid excretion.

questions.title: Respiratory system in the control of blood pH
questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct about the respiratory system as a control system for blood pH?

options.A: It is the most rapid of all the pH control systems
options.B: It is the least potent control system of pH
options.C: It controls pH by adjusting the arterial PCO2
options.D: It controls pH by adjusting the plasma bicarbonate concentration

explanations.A: Incorrect. The chemical buffer systems act essentially instantaneously and are the most rapid line of defence; the respiratory system responds within minutes, so it is fast but not the most rapid.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The respiratory system is actually quite powerful (about one to two times the buffering power of all the chemical buffers combined); the kidney is the slowest but most potent long-term regulator.
explanations.C: Correct. The lungs regulate pH by altering alveolar ventilation, which sets the arterial PCO2 and hence the carbonic acid concentration of the blood. Increasing ventilation blows off CO2 and raises pH, while hypoventilation retains CO2 and lowers pH. By adjusting PCO2 the respiratory system provides rapid, second-line control of acid-base balance between the instantaneous buffers and the slow renal response.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Adjusting the plasma bicarbonate concentration is the role of the kidney, not the lungs; the respiratory system operates on the CO2/carbonic-acid side of the buffer equation.

questions.learning_objective: State that the respiratory system controls pH by adjusting arterial PCO2 through ventilation.

questions.title: Condition most likely to cause metabolic alkalosis
questions.question: Which of the following conditions is most likely to cause metabolic alkalosis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Salicylate poisoning classically produces a mixed picture with a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (and an early respiratory alkalosis), not a metabolic alkalosis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Renal failure causes a metabolic acidosis because the failing kidney cannot excrete the daily acid load or regenerate bicarbonate.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Diabetic ketoacidosis is a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis due to the accumulation of ketoacids.
explanations.D: Correct. Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome) causes a metabolic alkalosis: aldosterone excess drives distal Na+ reabsorption coupled to increased H+ and K+ secretion, so the urine loses acid while bicarbonate is retained. The resulting hypokalaemia further shifts H+ into cells and enhances renal acid excretion, sustaining the alkalosis. This links a mineralocorticoid excess state to a rise in plasma bicarbonate and pH.

questions.learning_objective: Identify hyperaldosteronism (Conn's) as a cause of metabolic alkalosis and contrast it with acid-gaining states.
